questions.prompt: How many books make up the Catholic canon of Scripture in total?
questions.explanation: The Catholic canon includes 46 books of the Old Testament and 27 of the New Testament, for a total of 73 -- discerned by the Church through apostolic Tradition.
questions.hint: It's 46 Old Testament books plus 27 New Testament books.

citations.quote: It was by the apostolic Tradition that the Church discerned which writings are to be included in the list of the sacred books. This complete list is called the canon of Scripture.

questions.prompt: The Catechism teaches that Christians read the Old Testament in the light of what event?
choices: Christ crucified and risen
The fall of Jerusalem
The Babylonian exile alone
The building of the Temple
questions.correctAnswer: Christ crucified and risen
questions.explanation: CCC 129 teaches that 'Christians therefore read the Old Testament in the light of Christ crucified and risen' -- the whole of Scripture, Old and New, is read as one unified story fulfilled in Christ.
questions.hint: This is the central event of the New Testament, read back into the whole story.

citations.quote: Christians therefore read the Old Testament in the light of Christ crucified and risen.

questions.prompt: 'In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God' opens which book of the New Testament?
choices: The Gospel of John
The Gospel of Matthew
The Book of Revelation
The Letter to the Hebrews
questions.correctAnswer: The Gospel of John
questions.explanation: John 1:1 opens the Fourth Gospel with a profound statement of Christ's eternal divinity as the Word (Logos) who was with God and was God, later 'made flesh' in the Incarnation.
questions.hint: This Gospel's opening deliberately echoes the very first words of Genesis.

citations.quote: In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.

questions.prompt: The Bible is best described as:
choices: A library of many books, written by different human authors over centuries, with God as their ultimate author
A single book, written by one author in one sitting
A collection of myths with no historical value
A book written entirely in the last 200 years
questions.correctAnswer: A library of many books, written by different human authors over centuries, with God as their ultimate author
questions.explanation: God inspired the human authors of Scripture, who wrote in their own words, times, and literary forms -- true human authors, and yet God himself is the Bible's ultimate author.
questions.hint: Two authors are involved at once: many human ones, and one divine one.

citations.quote: God is the author of Sacred Scripture... The divinely revealed realities... have been written down under the inspiration of the Holy Spirit.

questions.prompt: True or False: The Bible was written by a single author, across a single generation.
questions.explanation: Scripture was composed by many human authors across roughly a thousand years, in different languages and literary forms -- yet it holds together as one unified word, since God inspired all of it.
questions.hint: Think of how many different named authors' names appear across the Bible's books.

citations.quote: God is the author of Sacred Scripture... The divinely revealed realities... have been written down under the inspiration of the Holy Spirit.

questions.prompt: The Bible is divided into two main parts: the Old Testament and the ____ Testament.
questions.correctAnswer: New
questions.explanation: The Old Testament records God's covenant with Israel before Christ; the New Testament records Christ's life and the apostolic Church founded on him.
questions.hint: It's the counterpart to 'Old.'

citations.quote: It was by the apostolic Tradition that the Church discerned which writings are to be included in the list of the sacred books. This complete list is called the canon of Scripture.

questions.prompt: The first five books of the Old Testament -- Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, and Deuteronomy -- are together called the:
choices: Torah (or Pentateuch)
Wisdom Literature
Minor Prophets
Historical Books
questions.correctAnswer: Torah (or Pentateuch)
questions.explanation: 'Pentateuch' comes from Greek for 'five scrolls'; 'Torah' is the Hebrew term, meaning 'instruction' or 'law' -- together these five books form the foundation of the whole Old Testament.
questions.hint: 'Penta-' is the Greek prefix for 'five.'

citations.quote: It was by the apostolic Tradition that the Church discerned which writings are to be included in the list of the sacred books. This complete list is called the canon of Scripture.

questions.prompt: True or False: The Book of Genesis contains two distinct creation accounts.
questions.explanation: Genesis opens with two complementary accounts of creation -- the six-day account in chapter 1, and a second account beginning in chapter 2 that focuses on the creation of man and woman.
questions.hint: Look closely at chapters 1 and 2 -- the story of creation is told a second time, from a different angle.

citations.quote: This is the story of the heavens and the earth at their creation. When the LORD God made the earth and the heavens

questions.prompt: God's covenant with Israel at Mount Sinai included the ____ Commandments, given to Moses.
questions.correctAnswer: Ten
questions.explanation: The Ten Commandments, given at Sinai, form the heart of the Old Covenant's moral law -- a law the Catechism treats as still binding in its substance under the New Covenant.
questions.hint: It's the same number of Commandments taught in every catechism class.

citations.quote: I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery; you shall have no other gods before me.

questions.prompt: The 'Major Prophets' of the Old Testament include Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, and:
choices: Daniel
Amos
Hosea
Malachi
questions.correctAnswer: Daniel
questions.explanation: The 'Major' and 'Minor' Prophets are distinguished by the length of their books, not by their relative importance -- Amos, Hosea, and Malachi belong instead to the twelve 'Minor Prophets.'
questions.hint: 'Major' here is about book length, not spiritual importance.

citations.quote: Through the prophets, God forms his people in the hope of salvation, in the expectation of a new and everlasting Covenant intended for all, to be written on their hearts.

questions.prompt: True or False: The prophets' central message was primarily to predict specific future events centuries in advance, with little concern for calling Israel back to covenant faithfulness in their own time.
questions.explanation: The prophets primarily called Israel to repentance and covenant fidelity in their own historical moment -- messianic hope for the future is part of their message, but not its whole focus.
questions.hint: Prophets were, first of all, preachers to their own generation, not just fortune-tellers for the future.

citations.quote: Jesus' call to conversion and penance, like that of the prophets before him, does not aim first at outward works... but at the conversion of the heart, interior conversion.

questions.prompt: Match each term to its meaning.

pairs.right: The first five books of the Bible
Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Daniel
A sacred bond God establishes with his people
Israel's deliverance from slavery in Egypt

questions.explanation: These four terms cover the backbone of Old Testament history -- its founding books, its major prophetic voices, its central theological concept, and its defining act of deliverance.
questions.hint: One is a group of books, one a group of prophets, one a theological concept, one a historical event.

citations.quote: I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery; you shall have no other gods before me.

questions.prompt: The first three Gospels -- Matthew, Mark, and Luke -- are called the 'Synoptic Gospels' because they:
choices: Share a similar structure, content, and viewpoint, and so can be 'seen together'
Were all written by the same single author
Are the only Gospels considered inspired
Were written after the Gospel of John
questions.correctAnswer: Share a similar structure, content, and viewpoint, and so can be 'seen together'
questions.explanation: 'Synoptic' comes from Greek meaning 'seen together' -- these three Gospels share substantial overlapping material and can be usefully compared side by side, unlike John's distinct approach.
questions.hint: 'Syn-optic' literally means 'together-view.'

citations.quote: the four Gospels... faithfully hand on what Jesus, the Son of God, while he lived among men, really did and taught for their eternal salvation.

questions.prompt: True or False: The Gospel of John is typically grouped together with Matthew, Mark, and Luke as one of the 'Synoptic Gospels.'
questions.explanation: John stands apart from the other three, with a distinct structure, style, and theological emphasis -- it is not counted among the Synoptics.
questions.hint: This is the one Gospel that stands apart from the other three, stylistically.

citations.quote: the four Gospels... faithfully hand on what Jesus, the Son of God, while he lived among men, really did and taught for their eternal salvation.

questions.prompt: The Catechism describes the Gospels as the 'heart of all the Scriptures' because they are our principal source for the life and ____ of the Incarnate Word.
questions.correctAnswer: teaching
questions.explanation: Everything else in Scripture -- Old and New Testament alike -- is read in relation to the Gospels, since they record Christ's own words and deeds most directly.
questions.hint: Alongside 'life,' this word is what the Gospels record about Christ's own words.

citations.quote: The Gospels are the heart of all the Scriptures 'because they are our principal source for the life and teaching of the Incarnate Word, our Saviour.'

questions.prompt: The Catechism describes the formation of the Gospels happening in three stages: the life and teaching of Jesus, the oral Tradition of the apostles, and finally:
choices: The Gospels being written down by the four evangelists
The Gospels being translated into Latin
The Council of Trent formally approving them
The invention of the printing press
questions.correctAnswer: The Gospels being written down by the four evangelists
questions.explanation: The evangelists, drawing on the earlier oral preaching of the apostolic Church, put this apostolic testimony into writing, 'selecting' and 'synthesizing' it for their particular communities.
questions.hint: This is the final stage, after Jesus' own ministry and the apostles' preaching about it.

citations.quote: the four Gospels... faithfully hand on what Jesus, the Son of God, while he lived among men, really did and taught for their eternal salvation.

questions.prompt: True or False: The Church requires every one of the four evangelists to have personally witnessed the entirety of Jesus' earthly ministry firsthand.
questions.explanation: The Gospels' reliability rests on their rootedness in apostolic testimony passed down faithfully, not on a requirement that every individual evangelist personally witnessed every event they recorded.
questions.hint: What matters is the Gospels' connection to apostolic testimony as a whole, not each author's personal presence at every event.

citations.quote: the four Gospels... faithfully hand on what Jesus, the Son of God, while he lived among men, really did and taught for their eternal salvation.

questions.prompt: Match each Gospel to a distinguishing note about it.

pairs.right: Written with a strongly Jewish audience and Old Testament fulfillment in mind
Shortest Gospel, fast-paced, emphasizing Christ's suffering servanthood
Emphasizes mercy, the poor, and salvation's universal reach
Distinct in style, emphasizing Christ's divinity and 'I am' statements

questions.explanation: Each evangelist writes with his own emphasis and audience in mind, while all four together present one coherent portrait of Christ.
questions.hint: One is Jewish-focused, one is fast and Passion-focused, one favors the poor, one is theologically distinct.

citations.quote: The Gospels are the heart of all the Scriptures 'because they are our principal source for the life and teaching of the Incarnate Word, our Saviour.'

questions.prompt: The largest single block of New Testament letters was written by:
choices: St. Paul
St. Peter
St. John
St. James
questions.correctAnswer: St. Paul
questions.explanation: Paul's letters to various churches and individuals -- Romans, Corinthians, Galatians, and many more -- make up the largest portion of the New Testament's epistolary literature.
questions.hint: This apostle's missionary journeys generated letters to many of the churches he founded.

citations.quote: Paul, a slave of Christ Jesus, called to be an apostle and set apart for the gospel of God

questions.prompt: True or False: The Letter to the Romans is widely regarded as containing Paul's most systematic presentation of the Gospel and the doctrine of justification.
questions.explanation: Romans opens with Paul's programmatic statement that he is 'not ashamed of the gospel,' since 'the righteous shall live by faith' -- launching one of Scripture's most sustained theological arguments.
questions.hint: This letter is often called Paul's theological masterwork.

citations.quote: For I am not ashamed of the gospel. It is the power of God for the salvation of everyone who believes... For in it is revealed the righteousness of God from faith to faith; as it is written, 'The one who is righteous by faith will live.'

questions.prompt: The Letter to the Hebrews presents Christ as the perfect and eternal ____ Priest, superior to the Levitical priesthood of the Old Covenant.
questions.correctAnswer: High
questions.explanation: Hebrews argues at length that Christ's priesthood, offered once for all, fulfills and surpasses the repeated sacrifices of the Old Covenant's priesthood.
questions.hint: This title pairs with 'priest' to describe the very highest priestly office.

citations.quote: We have a great high priest who has passed through the heavens, Jesus, the Son of God... one who has similarly been tested in every way, yet without sin.

questions.prompt: The 'Catholic Epistles' (James, 1-2 Peter, 1-3 John, Jude) are called 'Catholic' meaning:
choices: Universal or general, addressed broadly rather than to one specific local church
Written exclusively by popes
Approved only at the Council of Trent
Written in Latin rather than Greek
questions.correctAnswer: Universal or general, addressed broadly rather than to one specific local church
questions.explanation: Unlike Paul's letters, which typically address a specific community (Rome, Corinth, Galatia), these letters are addressed more broadly -- hence 'catholic,' meaning 'universal.'
questions.hint: 'Catholic' here carries its original Greek meaning -- 'according to the whole,' or universal.

citations.quote: James, a slave of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ, to the twelve tribes in the dispersion, greetings.

questions.prompt: True or False: The Letter of James teaches that faith without works is dead.
questions.explanation: James 2:17 states plainly: 'faith of itself, if it does not have works, is dead.' The letter insists genuine faith must show itself alive through concrete action.
questions.hint: This is one of the most direct statements in the New Testament connecting faith and action.

citations.quote: So also faith of itself, if it does not have works, is dead.

questions.prompt: Match each letter to its key theme.

pairs.right: Justification by grace through faith, systematically explained
Christ as the eternal High Priest
Faith must be shown alive through works
God is love, and love of neighbor flows from love of God

questions.explanation: Each New Testament letter addresses its own pressing pastoral concern, together forming a rich theological witness alongside the Gospels.
questions.hint: One is about justification, one about priesthood, one about works, one about love.

citations.quote: For I am not ashamed of the gospel. It is the power of God for the salvation of everyone who believes... For in it is revealed the righteousness of God from faith to faith; as it is written, 'The one who is righteous by faith will live.'
So also faith of itself, if it does not have works, is dead.

questions.prompt: The Catechism lists several senses of Scripture beyond the literal sense. Together these additional senses are called the:
choices: Spiritual senses (allegorical, moral, and anagogical)
Historical senses
Apocryphal senses
Vernacular senses
questions.correctAnswer: Spiritual senses (allegorical, moral, and anagogical)
questions.explanation: Beyond the literal sense (what the words directly mean), Catholic tradition reads Scripture for its spiritual senses -- how it points to Christ, teaches right action, and points toward our final destiny.
questions.hint: Three senses, all beyond the plain literal meaning of the words.

citations.quote: According to an ancient tradition, one can distinguish between two senses of Scripture: the literal and the spiritual, the latter being subdivided into the allegorical, moral and anagogical senses.

questions.prompt: True or False: The 'literal sense' of Scripture, in Catholic interpretation, means always reading every passage as a strict, scientifically precise historical report, regardless of its literary form.
questions.explanation: The literal sense means the meaning conveyed by the words themselves, discovered through sound interpretation that respects the author's own literary form -- poetry, parable, and historical narrative are all read according to what they actually are.
questions.hint: The literal sense respects what kind of writing a passage actually is -- poem, parable, history, and so on.

citations.quote: The literal sense is the meaning conveyed by the words of Scripture and discovered by exegesis, following the rules of sound interpretation.

questions.prompt: The Catechism teaches that Sacred Scripture must be read and interpreted 'in the light of the same ____' by which it was written -- that is, with the guidance of the Holy Spirit.
questions.correctAnswer: Spirit
questions.explanation: Because the Holy Spirit inspired Scripture's human authors, faithful interpretation requires reading it in that same Spirit, within the living Tradition of the Church that first received it.
questions.hint: This is the same divine Person who inspired the biblical authors in the first place.

citations.quote: Sacred Scripture must be read and interpreted in the light of the same Spirit by whom it was written.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is NOT one of the Catechism's three criteria for interpreting Scripture 'in accordance with the Spirit'?
choices: Purely private interpretation, independent of the Church's living Tradition
Attention to the content and unity of the whole of Scripture
Reading Scripture within the living Tradition of the Church
Attention to the analogy of faith
questions.correctAnswer: Purely private interpretation, independent of the Church's living Tradition
questions.explanation: The Catechism's three actual criteria all situate the individual reader within the Church's living Tradition and the coherence of the whole faith -- not apart from it.
questions.hint: Three of these four criteria all point back to the Church's own living Tradition; one explicitly cuts against it.

citations.quote: Be especially attentive 'to the content and unity of the whole Scripture'... read the Scripture within 'the living Tradition of the whole Church'... be attentive to the analogy of faith.

questions.prompt: True or False: The Catechism teaches that all the books and parts of Scripture are one, because all of Scripture is inspired by one and the same God.
questions.explanation: This is the first of the Catechism's criteria for interpreting Scripture -- reading with attention to the content and unity of the whole, since one divine author stands behind every book.
questions.hint: This is about Scripture's underlying unity, despite its many human authors and books.

citations.quote: Be especially attentive 'to the content and unity of the whole Scripture,' [since] Scripture is a unity by reason of the unity of God's plan, of which Christ Jesus is the center and heart.

questions.prompt: Match each sense of Scripture to its focus.

pairs.right: The meaning intended by the human author's own words
How events and figures point to Christ
How Scripture teaches us to act justly
How realities point toward our eternal destiny

questions.explanation: These four senses, working together, let the same passage of Scripture speak on multiple levels at once -- what it plainly says, and what it points beyond itself toward.
questions.hint: One sense is about the plain words; three others point toward Christ, right action, or eternity.

citations.quote: According to an ancient tradition, one can distinguish between two senses of Scripture: the literal and the spiritual, the latter being subdivided into the allegorical, moral and anagogical senses.

questions.prompt: Trent's Fourth Session (1546) formally closed the Old Testament canon, affirming books the Reformers rejected as a shorter, 'protocanonical-only' list. What does 'deuterocanonical' mean, applied to books like Tobit, Judith, and Wisdom?
choices: Books whose canonicity was affirmed later and more explicitly than the protocanonical books, not books added or invented at Trent
Books that were written after the New Testament closed
Books accepted by Protestants but rejected by Catholics
Books that were never used in the Church before 1546
questions.correctAnswer: Books whose canonicity was affirmed later and more explicitly than the protocanonical books, not books added or invented at Trent
questions.explanation: 'Deuterocanonical' (literally 'second canon') names books whose place in the canon received more explicit, formal affirmation later in Church history than the 'protocanonical' books, not books that were newly invented or added at Trent -- these books were already read as Scripture in the Church's ancient liturgical use well before Trent formally closed the question against Reformation-era challenges.
questions.hint: The prefix means 'second,' referring to the timing of formal affirmation, not a lesser status or later composition.

citations.quote: [The Synod] receives and venerates with an equal affection of piety and reverence all the books both of the Old and New Testament.

questions.prompt: Dei Verbum 11 states that Scripture teaches 'the truth which God wanted put into the sacred writings for the sake of our salvation.' How does this precise formula differ from a flat claim that 'the Bible has no errors of any kind'?
choices: It locates inerrancy specifically in what God intended for our salvation, not in every incidental historical or scientific detail a text happens to mention
It means the Bible actually does contain doctrinal errors that the Church has chosen to overlook
It applies only to the New Testament, exempting the Old Testament from any inerrancy claim
It was written specifically to reverse Trent's teaching on inspiration
questions.correctAnswer: It locates inerrancy specifically in what God intended for our salvation, not in every incidental historical or scientific detail a text happens to mention
questions.explanation: Dei Verbum's formula is precise: the truth God wanted recorded for our salvation is what Scripture teaches without error, which is a narrower and more careful claim than an unqualified 'no errors of any kind' -- avoiding both a denial of biblical truth and an overreaching claim about every incidental detail.
questions.hint: Look closely at the phrase 'for the sake of our salvation' -- that's doing real, restrictive work in the sentence.

citations.quote: The books of Scripture firmly, faithfully, and without error teach the truth that God, for the sake of our salvation, wished to be put in writing in Holy Writ.

questions.prompt: The 'Two-Source Hypothesis' explaining the Synoptic Gospels' close verbal overlap proposes that Matthew and Luke each drew on which two sources?
choices: The Gospel of Mark and a hypothetical sayings collection called 'Q'
Two independent eyewitness accounts, neither of which survives today
The Gospel of John and an otherwise unknown Hebrew Gospel
Each other, with no third source involved at all
questions.correctAnswer: The Gospel of Mark and a hypothetical sayings collection called 'Q'
questions.explanation: The Two-Source Hypothesis, built on the observation of Markan priority (Mark was written first and used as a source by the other two), proposes that Matthew and Luke each independently drew on Mark plus a hypothetical sayings source scholars call 'Q' (from German 'Quelle,' source) to explain material they share that isn't in Mark.
questions.hint: One of the two sources is a Gospel you already know; the other is a hypothesis, not a surviving document.

citations.quote: the four Gospels... faithfully hand on what Jesus, the Son of God, while he lived among men, really did and taught for their eternal salvation.

questions.prompt: True or False: Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus, two of the oldest surviving nearly-complete Greek manuscripts of the Bible, are cited by scholars as physical evidence for how the biblical text was actually transmitted, not merely referenced as trivia.
questions.explanation: These two 4th-century codices are among the most important witnesses used in textual criticism -- comparing their readings against later manuscripts is how scholars trace the text's transmission history and identify where later copies added, omitted, or altered material.
questions.hint: These aren't just old and famous -- they're actively used as evidence in real scholarly arguments about the text.

citations.quote: It was by the apostolic Tradition that the Church discerned which writings are to be included in the list of the sacred books. This complete list is called the canon of Scripture.

questions.prompt: The Synod of Rome (382), sometimes associated with a 'Decree of Damasus,' is cited by historians as an early ____ to the canon's shape -- not as the definitive closing act, which is properly credited to Trent's Fourth Session (1546).
questions.correctAnswer: witness
questions.explanation: Historians debate the exact canon-list content attributed to the Synod of Rome (382), so it's cited carefully as an early witness to a canon list resembling the later one, not as the definitive, formal closing of the canon -- that formal closure, in response to the Reformation's shorter list, belongs to Trent's Fourth Session (1546).
questions.hint: This word describes something that testifies to an already-forming reality, without being the final, formal act itself.

citations.quote: [The Synod] receives and venerates with an equal affection of piety and reverence all the books both of the Old and New Testament.

questions.prompt: Match each term from this level to its precise meaning.

pairs.right: Formally affirmed later and more explicitly than the protocanonical books, not invented at Trent
Matthew and Luke each drawing on Mark plus a hypothetical sayings source called 'Q'
Physical 4th-century manuscript evidence used in tracing the text's transmission
A scholarly question distinct from, and not decisive for, the Church's judgment of canonicity and inspiration

questions.explanation: Each of these terms replaces a lay paraphrase with the Church's or scholarship's own precise vocabulary, wired to the specific argument or evidence that motivated it.
questions.hint: Two of these concern the Old Testament canon and text; two concern the New Testament's composition.

citations.quote: It was by the apostolic Tradition that the Church discerned which writings are to be included in the list of the sacred books. This complete list is called the canon of Scripture.

questions.prompt: An objector says, 'The Bible gets a scientific or historical detail wrong somewhere, so it can't be inspired.' Using Dei Verbum 11's precise formula, what is the accurate response?
choices: Inerrancy applies to the truth God wanted recorded for our salvation, not necessarily to every incidental scientific or historical detail a text happens to mention
The objection is correct, and the Church has quietly abandoned any claim to inerrancy
Inerrancy means every single statement in Scripture must be scientifically precise by modern standards
The objection can only be answered by denying that the Bible mentions any historical events at all
questions.correctAnswer: Inerrancy applies to the truth God wanted recorded for our salvation, not necessarily to every incidental scientific or historical detail a text happens to mention
questions.explanation: Level 6 already fixed this precise formula: Dei Verbum locates inerrancy in the saving truth God wanted conveyed, not in a modern textbook's standard of precision for every incidental detail -- an ancient author's phenomenological description of the natural world, for instance, isn't a scientific claim the text is staking its inspired status on.
questions.hint: Look back to level 6's precise wording of what Dei Verbum 11 actually claims.

citations.quote: The books of Scripture firmly, faithfully, and without error teach the truth that God, for the sake of our salvation, wished to be put in writing in Holy Writ.

questions.prompt: An objector says, 'Catholics added seven books to the Bible.' Using the canon history from level 6, what is the accurate reframing of this claim?
choices: The Reformers removed books from an already-received canon in the 16th century; Trent's 1546 session formally reaffirmed the longer list the Church had already used, rather than the Church adding anything new
The claim is entirely accurate exactly as stated -- the Catholic Church added the books at the Council of Trent
Neither Catholics nor Protestants have ever had a fixed Old Testament canon
The seven books in question were written after the New Testament closed
questions.correctAnswer: The Reformers removed books from an already-received canon in the 16th century; Trent's 1546 session formally reaffirmed the longer list the Church had already used, rather than the Church adding anything new
questions.explanation: The historical direction runs the opposite way from the objection: these books were already part of the Church's received and liturgically used canon well before the Reformation. Trent's Fourth Session formally reaffirmed that existing longer list in response to 16th-century Reformers removing these books, rather than the Church newly adding them.
questions.hint: This is a direction-of-history problem -- ask which side actually changed an existing, received list.

citations.quote: [The Synod] receives and venerates with an equal affection of piety and reverence all the books both of the Old and New Testament.

questions.prompt: An objector says, 'The Gospels copied each other, so they aren't independent eyewitness testimony.' Using Markan priority and the Church's three-stage Gospel formation process (CCC 126), what is the accurate response?
choices: Literary dependence in composition and apostolic reliability in content aren't in tension -- later evangelists drawing on earlier written and oral apostolic tradition is exactly the process CCC 126 describes, not a discovery that undermines it
The Gospels have no literary relationship whatsoever, and any appearance of overlap is coincidental
Literary dependence proves the Gospels are entirely fictional
CCC 126 was written specifically to deny that Mark was used as a source by the other Gospels
questions.correctAnswer: Literary dependence in composition and apostolic reliability in content aren't in tension -- later evangelists drawing on earlier written and oral apostolic tradition is exactly the process CCC 126 describes, not a discovery that undermines it
questions.explanation: CCC 126 describes a three-stage formation process -- the life and teaching of Jesus, the apostles' oral preaching, and the evangelists' later written composition drawing on those earlier stages. Mark being used as a source by Matthew and Luke is exactly this kind of continuity with apostolic tradition, not evidence of fabrication or independent invention.
questions.hint: The three-stage process in CCC 126 already accounts for later written Gospels drawing on earlier apostolic material.

citations.quote: the four Gospels... faithfully hand on what Jesus, the Son of God, while he lived among men, really did and taught for their eternal salvation.

questions.prompt: A sola scriptura objection claims, 'The Bible alone is a sufficient and self-interpreting rule of faith, with no need for the Church's authority.' Using the interpretive criteria already covered in this topic (living Tradition, the analogy of faith), what is the accurate response?
choices: Scripture itself requires correct interpretation within the living Tradition and the analogy of faith -- a text that different readers interpret in contradictory ways cannot function as a wholly self-interpreting rule without an authoritative interpreter
The Church agrees Scripture is entirely self-interpreting and needs no additional guidance whatsoever
The analogy of faith and living Tradition are modern Catholic inventions with no basis in how the earliest Christians read Scripture
Sola scriptura is correct, and the Catholic Church has quietly adopted it since Vatican II
questions.correctAnswer: Scripture itself requires correct interpretation within the living Tradition and the analogy of faith -- a text that different readers interpret in contradictory ways cannot function as a wholly self-interpreting rule without an authoritative interpreter
questions.explanation: The historical fact of thousands of different, mutually contradictory interpretations arising from sola scriptura is itself evidence against the claim that Scripture is simply self-interpreting -- the Church's teaching is that Scripture must be read within the living Tradition and 'analogy of faith' (the coherence of all revealed truths with each other), guided by the Magisterium's authority to interpret authentically.
questions.hint: The strongest evidence against 'self-interpreting' is simply how many contradictory readings the same text has actually produced.

citations.quote: Read the Scripture within 'the living Tradition of the whole Church'... it is the Holy Spirit who gives her the spiritual interpretation of the Scripture.

questions.prompt: True or False: The apparent tension between James 2:24 ('a person is justified by works and not by faith alone') and Romans 3:28 ('a person is justified by faith apart from works of the law') is resolved by recognizing the two authors use 'faith' and 'works' in different senses suited to the specific errors each is correcting, not by declaring one passage simply wrong.
questions.explanation: Paul in Romans is countering a reliance on the Mosaic law's ritual works as a means of justification apart from faith in Christ, while James is countering an empty, inert 'faith' that produces no actual charity or good works -- read according to each author's specific target and literary context, the two passages address different errors rather than contradicting each other.
questions.hint: The key move is asking what specific error each author is actually correcting, not assuming both must use the same word the same way.

citations.quote: For we consider that a person is justified by faith apart from works of the law.
See how a person is justified by works and not by faith alone.

pairs.left: 'The Bible gets a scientific detail wrong'
pairs.right: Inerrancy covers the saving truth God intended, not every incidental detail
The Reformers removed books from an already-received canon; Trent reaffirmed it

questions.prompt: Per Dei Verbum 12 and the Pontifical Biblical Commission's 1993 document 'The Interpretation of the Bible in the Church,' what is the historical-critical method's legitimate contribution, and what is its limit when used alone?
choices: It legitimately illuminates authorial intent and historical/literary context, but risks missing a text's full theological meaning if it excludes the light of faith and Tradition
It has no legitimate use in Catholic biblical scholarship and is formally condemned
It fully replaces the need for any theological or spiritual reading of Scripture
It applies only to the New Testament, never to the Old Testament
questions.correctAnswer: It legitimately illuminates authorial intent and historical/literary context, but risks missing a text's full theological meaning if it excludes the light of faith and Tradition
questions.explanation: The 1993 PBC document affirms the historical-critical method's real, positive contribution to understanding a text's original context and intended meaning, while cautioning that used in isolation -- without the complementary light of faith, Tradition, and the Church's living interpretation -- it risks missing dimensions of meaning Dei Verbum 12 says belong to a text inspired by God for the Church's ongoing life.
questions.hint: This is a 'legitimate but incomplete alone' answer, not a flat approval or rejection.

citations.quote: The interpreter must investigate what meaning the sacred writer intended to express and actually expressed in particular circumstances by using contemporary literary forms.

questions.prompt: True or False: The Alexandrian school's emphasis on allegory and the Antiochene school's emphasis on literal-historical restraint represent two legitimate but different accents within the same fourfold-sense framework, not a simple right-versus-wrong pair.
questions.explanation: Both schools operated within the Church's broader tradition of reading Scripture according to multiple senses (literal, allegorical, moral, anagogical); Alexandria leaned toward drawing out the allegorical and typological, while Antioch leaned toward historical and grammatical restraint -- legitimate differences of emphasis, not one school being simply orthodox and the other simply in error.
questions.hint: This is a difference of emphasis within a shared framework, similar to other legitimate diversities already seen in this app.

citations.quote: one can distinguish between two senses of Scripture: the literal and the spiritual, the latter being subdivided into the allegorical, moral and anagogical senses.

questions.prompt: Given the binding of Isaac (Genesis 22), which correctly matches a historical-critical reading to its characteristic concern, as distinct from an allegorical reading's concern?
choices: Historical-critical: the passage's ancient Near Eastern context and the practice of child sacrifice it stands against; allegorical: Isaac as a type of Christ carrying wood to his own sacrifice
Historical-critical and allegorical readings ask exactly the same question and reach exactly the same conclusion
Historical-critical readings are concerned only with allegory; allegorical readings are concerned only with historical context
Neither reading has any legitimate basis in Catholic biblical scholarship
questions.correctAnswer: Historical-critical: the passage's ancient Near Eastern context and the practice of child sacrifice it stands against; allegorical: Isaac as a type of Christ carrying wood to his own sacrifice
questions.explanation: A historical-critical reading situates the passage against its ancient Near Eastern background, noting how it stands against child sacrifice practiced by surrounding cultures; an allegorical/typological reading, already licensed by the fourfold-sense framework, sees Isaac carrying the wood for his own sacrifice as prefiguring Christ carrying his cross -- both are legitimate readings operating at different levels of the text's meaning.
questions.hint: One reading looks outward to ancient context; the other looks forward to how the passage prefigures Christ.

citations.quote: We can acquire a more profound understanding of events by recognizing their significance in Christ; thus the crossing of the Red Sea is a sign or type of Christ's victory and also of Christian Baptism.

questions.prompt: The Documentary Hypothesis proposes that the Pentateuch was compiled from four source traditions (J, E, D, P) rather than written entirely by Moses alone. Per the Pontifical Biblical Commission's 1948 letter to Cardinal Suhard, what is the Church's actual stance on this hypothesis?
choices: It is permitted as a legitimate scholarly hypothesis for Catholic exegetes to discuss and weigh, not binding doctrine that must be accepted or rejected as a matter of faith
It has been formally condemned as heretical
It has been formally declared the Church's official teaching on the Pentateuch's authorship
It applies only to the book of Genesis, not the rest of the Pentateuch
questions.correctAnswer: It is permitted as a legitimate scholarly hypothesis for Catholic exegetes to discuss and weigh, not binding doctrine that must be accepted or rejected as a matter of faith
questions.explanation: The 1948 PBC letter to Cardinal Suhard acknowledged the value of source-critical study of the Pentateuch's composition history while affirming Mosaic authorship in a broader, substantial sense (Moses as the tradition's authoritative source, even if later editors compiled and shaped the final text) -- treating the specific documentary details as an open scholarly question, not a matter the faith requires settling one way or the other.
questions.hint: This is the same pattern as level 6's point about disputed Pauline authorship -- a scholarly question the Church leaves open rather than dogmatically resolving.

citations.reference: Pontifical Biblical Commission, Letter to Cardinal Suhard (1948)

questions.prompt: True or False: Whether the Alexandrian or Antiochene emphasis best serves preaching today is a contested-within-orthodoxy methodological question, while the claim that Scripture has a literal, allegorical, moral, and anagogical sense at all is settled Catholic teaching, not an open question.
questions.explanation: The fourfold-sense framework itself -- that Scripture bears these different levels of meaning -- is settled Catholic teaching (CCC 115-119); which historical school's emphasis is more pastorally useful for preaching in a given context is a live, legitimate methodological question, not a doctrinal one. Confusing the two would either wrongly dogmatize a preference or wrongly relativize a settled teaching.
questions.hint: One of these two claims is about whether something exists at all; the other is about which emphasis works best in practice.

questions.prompt: The Antiochene school's literal-historical hermeneutic is sometimes historically associated with the christological tendencies later condemned in Nestorius. What is the correct way to state this connection?
choices: A historical association scholars debate the strength of, not a claim that Antiochene exegesis as such is doctrinally erroneous
A settled dogmatic fact: the Antiochene school was formally condemned as heretical alongside Nestorius
No connection exists at all between the school and the later controversy
The Antiochene school was founded specifically to promote Nestorius's teaching
questions.correctAnswer: A historical association scholars debate the strength of, not a claim that Antiochene exegesis as such is doctrinally erroneous
questions.explanation: Historians note a real historical and educational connection between the Antiochene exegetical tradition and figures later associated with Nestorianism, but the exegetical method itself was never formally condemned -- level 8 already affirmed Antiochene literal-historical reading as a legitimate emphasis. This connection is a historical-judgment question about influence and association, not a doctrinal verdict on the method.
questions.hint: Look back to level 8 -- the Antiochene method itself was never declared erroneous there, and that hasn't changed.

questions.prompt: The Church's typological reading of Isaac as a foreshadowing of Christ (CCC 128-130) can be compared with, but is distinct from, rabbinic exegetical methods like midrash. How should this comparison be correctly tagged?
choices: The typological reading itself is settled Catholic teaching; the comparative claim about how it relates to rabbinic method is a historical-judgment question about interpretive history, not a doctrinal one
Both the typological reading and the historical comparison are equally unsettled, open questions
The comparison proves rabbinic and Catholic exegesis are identical methods with no real difference
Typology has been abandoned by the Church in favor of purely historical-critical reading
questions.correctAnswer: The typological reading itself is settled Catholic teaching; the comparative claim about how it relates to rabbinic method is a historical-judgment question about interpretive history, not a doctrinal one
questions.explanation: CCC 128-130 affirms typological reading (Christ prefigured in Old Testament persons and events) as settled Catholic teaching. Comparing this method historically to rabbinic techniques like midrash and pesher is a separate, historical-critical question about interpretive traditions and their relationships -- worth exploring, but not itself a doctrinal claim requiring the same certainty.
questions.hint: Two different kinds of claims are being made here -- keep them separate rather than treating both with the same level of certainty.

citations.quote: The Church... has illuminated the unity of the divine plan in the two Testaments through typology, which discerns in God's works of the Old Covenant prefigurations of what he accomplished in the fullness of time in the person of his incarnate Son.

questions.prompt: The 'New Perspective on Paul' (associated with scholars like E.P. Sanders and N.T. Wright) offers a different account of what Paul means by 'works of the law' in Romans and Galatians than the traditional Augustinian/Reformation-era reading. How should this scholarly debate be correctly treated?
choices: As a genuinely contested-within-orthodoxy scholarly debate, not a question the Magisterium has adjudicated by declaring one side simply correct
As a debate the Catholic Church has officially settled in favor of the New Perspective
As a debate the Catholic Church has officially settled in favor of the traditional reading
As a heretical position that has been formally condemned
questions.correctAnswer: As a genuinely contested-within-orthodoxy scholarly debate, not a question the Magisterium has adjudicated by declaring one side simply correct
questions.explanation: The New Perspective (developed in works like Sanders's Paul and Palestinian Judaism, 1977, and Wright's What Saint Paul Really Said, 1997) proposes that Paul's 'works of the law' language responds primarily to Jewish covenantal boundary markers rather than a generic legalistic earning of salvation. This remains a live, contested scholarly conversation connecting back to this topic's own Letters and Epistles level, not a question the Magisterium has adjudicated in favor of either side.
questions.hint: Prerequisite: this topic's own Letters and Epistles level, where Paul's letters were first introduced.

citations.quote: For we consider that a person is justified by faith apart from works of the law.

questions.prompt: Dei Verbum teaches that Scripture and Tradition together form 'one sacred deposit of the word of God' (CCC 80-82). How does this connect to what this topic's own 'Reading as the Church' level already established about interpretation?
choices: Since Scripture and Tradition form a single deposit rather than two separate sources, the Church's authoritative interpretation of Scripture is not an outside imposition on the text but engagement with the same one deposit Scripture itself belongs to
Scripture and Tradition are two entirely separate and potentially conflicting sources of revelation
Tradition is a merely human custom with no real doctrinal authority
This teaching reverses everything the 'Reading as the Church' level established about interpretation
questions.correctAnswer: Since Scripture and Tradition form a single deposit rather than two separate sources, the Church's authoritative interpretation of Scripture is not an outside imposition on the text but engagement with the same one deposit Scripture itself belongs to
questions.explanation: CCC 80-82's 'one sacred deposit' teaching is the doctrinal foundation for why the Church interpreting Scripture within living Tradition (already covered in this topic's 'Reading as the Church' level) isn't adding something foreign to the text -- Scripture and Tradition flow from the same one wellspring and are received together by the Church.
questions.hint: Prerequisite: this topic's own 'Reading as the Church' level.

citations.quote: Sacred Tradition and Sacred Scripture... flowing out from the same divine well-spring, come together in some fashion to form one thing and move towards the same goal.

questions.explanation: The Liturgy and Mass topic's coverage of the lectionary's structured, multi-year cycle expresses the same underlying conviction this topic teaches about Scripture's God-given authority and completeness -- the Church's public proclamation of Scripture is organized precisely so that the full range of the inspired text, not a curated favorites list, forms believers over time.

questions.prompt: The Comma Johanneum (1 John 5:7-8), a Trinitarian formula absent from the earliest Greek manuscripts, is omitted from modern critical texts and translations. Why doesn't its absence undermine the doctrine of the Trinity?
choices: The doctrine of the Trinity rests on the wider testimony of Scripture and the Church's doctrinal development, not on this one textually late and disputed verse
The doctrine of the Trinity has no other scriptural basis and is now considered unsupported
The Comma Johanneum's removal proves the doctrine of the Trinity was invented in the medieval period
Modern critical texts have restored the Comma Johanneum as authentic
questions.correctAnswer: The doctrine of the Trinity rests on the wider testimony of Scripture and the Church's doctrinal development, not on this one textually late and disputed verse
questions.explanation: The Comma Johanneum appears to be a later Latin textual addition absent from the earliest Greek manuscript tradition, and modern critical editions and most translations note or omit it accordingly. The doctrine of the Trinity does not depend on this one contested verse -- it rests on the broader witness of Scripture (the baptismal formula, Johannine and Pauline texts) read through the Church's doctrinal development across the early councils.
questions.hint: One textually disputed verse being set aside doesn't remove an entire doctrine's much wider foundation.

questions.prompt: Mark 16:9-20 (the 'longer ending'), absent from Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus, raises a real textual question. What is the Church's actual resolution of its status?
choices: The longer ending is received as canonical and inspired through the Church's long liturgical and traditional use, a question distinct from the separate historical question of its authorial origin
The longer ending has been formally removed from the canon by the Magisterium
Its absence from two manuscripts proves the entire Gospel of Mark is unreliable
The textual question has never been acknowledged by any Church document
questions.correctAnswer: The longer ending is received as canonical and inspired through the Church's long liturgical and traditional use, a question distinct from the separate historical question of its authorial origin
questions.explanation: The Church distinguishes the question of a passage's canonical and inspired status -- settled by its consistent reception and liturgical use across the Church's history -- from the separate historical-critical question of exactly how or by whom it was originally composed. Mark 16:9-20 remains part of the canonical text on this basis, regardless of what textual criticism concludes about its origin.
questions.hint: This is the same move as level 6's point about disputed Pauline authorship not being decisive for canonicity -- applied here to an ending rather than a whole letter.

citations.quote: It was by the apostolic Tradition that the Church discerned which writings are to be included in the list of the sacred books. This complete list is called the canon of Scripture.

questions.prompt: The pericope adulterae (John 7:53-8:11, the woman caught in adultery) has an unsettled manuscript history, appearing in different locations in different early manuscript traditions. Why doesn't this compromise its canonical status or continued use?
choices: Its canonical and liturgical reception by the Church, sustained across centuries, does not require settling every detail of its precise manuscript placement history
The passage has been formally removed from all modern Bibles
An unsettled placement history proves the event it describes never happened
The Church has never used this passage in preaching or liturgy because of the textual uncertainty
questions.correctAnswer: Its canonical and liturgical reception by the Church, sustained across centuries, does not require settling every detail of its precise manuscript placement history
questions.explanation: Like the Markan ending, the pericope adulterae's exact manuscript history (which Gospel it originally belonged with, if any single original placement can even be identified) is a real textual-critical question, but the Church's canonical and liturgical reception of the passage does not hinge on resolving every detail of that history -- the passage remains part of the canonical Gospel of John and continues in ordinary liturgical and homiletic use.
questions.hint: This follows the same pattern as the Markan ending question -- reception and canonicity are distinct from unsettled placement history.

citations.quote: It was by the apostolic Tradition that the Church discerned which writings are to be included in the list of the sacred books. This complete list is called the canon of Scripture.

questions.prompt: Scholars use critical editions like Nestle-Aland's Novum Testamentum Graece and the Biblia Hebraica Stuttgartensia, while the Roman liturgy uses the Church's own Nova Vulgata (1979) as its official reference text. Why can the Church use a different 'typical edition' for worship without contradicting the scholarship?
choices: A liturgical typical edition serves the Church's need for a single, stable, authoritative text for public worship, while critical editions serve ongoing textual-critical scholarship -- different purposes, not competing claims about which is 'true'
The Nova Vulgata rejects the findings of modern textual criticism entirely
Critical editions and the Nova Vulgata are identical documents under different names
The Church has declared textual criticism illegitimate for use in preparing liturgical texts
questions.correctAnswer: A liturgical typical edition serves the Church's need for a single, stable, authoritative text for public worship, while critical editions serve ongoing textual-critical scholarship -- different purposes, not competing claims about which is 'true'
questions.explanation: The Nova Vulgata, promulgated in 1979, actually draws on modern critical scholarship in its preparation while serving a specifically liturgical function: providing one stable, authoritative text for the Roman Rite's public worship. Critical editions like NA28 and BHS serve the different, ongoing purpose of tracking and weighing manuscript evidence -- the two coexist because they answer different needs, not because one refutes the other.
questions.hint: Ask what job each edition is actually doing, rather than assuming only one can be 'the real Bible.'

questions.prompt: A friend says, 'I heard verses were added to the Bible later -- doesn't that mean it's unreliable?' Using everything this level has covered, which is the most accurate, sayable response?
choices: A small number of specific passages have a genuinely debated textual history, which scholars and the Church have long acknowledged openly -- but this is a world apart from the text as a whole being unreliable, since the vast majority of the text is solidly and consistently attested across thousands of manuscripts
No, this has never been acknowledged by any Christian scholar or Church document
Yes, this means the entire Bible cannot be trusted at all
The Church refuses to discuss this topic because it is too damaging to faith
questions.correctAnswer: A small number of specific passages have a genuinely debated textual history, which scholars and the Church have long acknowledged openly -- but this is a world apart from the text as a whole being unreliable, since the vast majority of the text is solidly and consistently attested across thousands of manuscripts
questions.explanation: The honest, sayable answer names the real textual questions (the Comma Johanneum, the Markan ending, the pericope adulterae) openly, exactly as this level has, while putting them in proportion: these are a handful of well-studied cases against a text overwhelmingly and consistently attested across an enormous body of manuscript evidence, openly discussed rather than hidden.
questions.hint: The strongest answer neither denies the real textual questions nor lets a few genuine cases stand in for the whole text's reliability.
